case_info.scenario: A woman in her late 60s presented to the emergency department after an episode of syncope. She described several other episodes occurring at rest over the past several weeks. She denied palpitations, chest pain, and shortness of breath. She was otherwise in excellent health and not taking any medications. She had no family history of syncope or sudden death. Her vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. The initial electrocardiogram (ECG) results were normal, but premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) were noted on telemetry. Shortly thereafter, 2 episodes of fast polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT), 30 minutes apart, were recorded, both lasting less than 4 seconds (Figure 1A). A repeat ECG showed PVCs (Figure 1B). Laboratory test results including serum potassium and magnesium as well as 3 serial troponin levels were normal. Echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic function without wall motion abnormalities or valvular abnormalities. Coronary angiography showed a 50% stenosis of the left circumflex artery. Instant wave-free ratio across the stenosis was 1.0.

case_info.caption: A, A continuous rhythm strip showing a short episode of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT), which is initiated by a short-coupled premature ventricular contraction (PVC) identical in morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring a few beats earlier. B, A subsequent electrocardiogram (ECG) showed frequent short-coupled premature ventricular contractions.
case_info.explanation: The ECG inFigure 1B shows normal sinus rhythm with a normal axis, sinus arrhythmia, nonspecific P wave abnormality, and minor nonspecific T wave changes. There are frequent uniform PVCs with a right bundle branch block morphology and a right superior axis. Retrograde P waves following the PVCs are noted. The PVCs are superimposed on the T waves, most notably in lead aVF (the PVCs start after the peak of the T wave), consistent with the R-on-T phenomenon, with a short coupling interval of approximately 330 milliseconds. PVCs with short coupling intervals have been shown to trigger PVT and ventricular fibrillation in patients with structurally normal hearts, which can lead to syncope and sudden cardiac death. The episodes of PVT shown inFigure 1A are initiated with a PVC that has an identical morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring few beats earlier. The QT interval is not prolonged. There is no coved ST-segment elevation in V1through V2to suggest Brugada syndrome. No ST-segment elevation precedes runs of PVT, ruling out coronary spasm as the etiology. Provocative drug testing is not helpful since there is no suspicion of Brugada syndrome or prolonged QT interval. Options C is therapy for long QT syndrome. Option D, PVC ablation, can be a complimentary treatment, but placement of a defibrillator is required to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death. The first mention of the association of the R-on-T phenomenon with malignant ventricular arrhythmias was by Fastier and Smirk1in 1948 (Figure 2). R waves interrupting T waves were described again in 17 patients by Smirk2in 1949, with several patients dying suddenly. Two more cases of Adams-Stocks attacks due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with apparently normal hearts were reported around the same time.3,4 PVCs are ubiquitous in the general population. In the Framingham Heart Study, PVCs or more complex ventricular arrhythmias were observed in 12% of participants without coronary artery disease monitored for just 1 hour.5Initially, it was thought that the prognosis of PVCs, in the absence of evident structural heart disease, was excellent. Later, the likelihood of cardiac mortality was reportedly double in patients with ventricular ectopy followed up for 10 years.6A PVC grading system, from 0 to 5, was introduced by Lown and Wolf7in 1971. An early PVC (R-on-T PVC) was graded at 5, denoting the highest risk. Lown and Wolf referenced the earlier work by Smirk,2but the grading system was gauged to assess the risk after myocardial infarction. Grade 2 to 4 A&B per the Lown and Wolf system are frequent PVCs, multiform PVCs, ventricular couplets and 3 or more PVCs in a row. High burden of PVCs and interpolated ones have been linked to cardiomyopathy in the absence of coronary artery disease. Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation was coined to describe the arrhythmia in an otherwise normal heart and is responsible for approximately 5% to 7% of cases of aborted cardiac arrest.8Short-coupled idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (SCIVF) is diagnosed in the presence of PVCs initiating PVT and fibrillation. A review of 86 patients with SCIVF showed the mean (SD) PVC coupling interval was 293 (50.5) milliseconds and less than 300 milliseconds in 48 patients.8As is likely in this case, the majority of PVC triggers of SCIVF originate from the Purkinje system. Long-term suppression of arrhythmias with oral medications was highest with quinidine (83.3%) followed by verapamil (50%). Ablation of PVC trigger was attempted in 55.8% and was successful in the acute phase in 83.3%.8 An implanted cardioverter/defibrillator was placed. Verapamil was started for suppression of PVCs. Ablation was planned if the patient had recurrence of arrhythmias. This patient had 1 episode of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia 3 months after initial presentation; it terminated without a shock. She had no other episodes over the ensuing 5 years.

dialogue_history.text: The most appropriate next step in management is to perform provocative drug testing with procainamide. Given the patient's episodes of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT) caused by short-coupled PVCs, this indicates a potential for a reentrant mechanism that could be provoked with a drug like procainamide to assess the substrate for arrhythmogenicity. Implanting a defibrillator may be premature without confirming the underlying cause, and while nadolol could provide antiarrhythmic effects, it does not address the immediate concern of identifying the arrhythmia mechanism. Ablation could be considered later, depending on the results of drug testing.

dialogue_history.text: Provocative drug testing with procainamide is not the standard initial step here. The clinical picture—recurrent syncope and short-coupled PVCs triggering polymorphic VT in a structurally normal heart—strongly points to short-coupled variant of torsades de pointes, which is a specific diagnosis, not a generic reentrant substrate. The priority is to initiate a beta-blocker like nadolol or consider quinidine, which is often effective, not to perform provocative testing that could be risky and is not first-line.

metadata.belief: The diagnosis is short-coupled variant of torsades de pointes, and the next management step is to start a beta-blocker (e.g., nadolol) or consider quinidine therapy.

We need to clarify that implementing nadolol without understanding the underlying mechanism may not be prudent in this context.

3 = Moderate workload

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Her vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. The initial electrocardiogram (ECG) results were normal, but premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) were noted on telemetry. Shortly thereafter, 2 episodes of fast polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT), 30 minutes apart, were recorded, both lasting less than 4 seconds (Figure 1A). A repeat ECG showed PVCs (Figure 1B). Laboratory test results including serum potassium and magnesium as well as 3 serial troponin levels were normal. Echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic function without wall motion abnormalities or valvular abnormalities. Coronary angiography showed a 50% stenosis of the left circumflex artery. Instant wave-free ratio across the stenosis was 1.0.

Implanting a defibrillator may be premature without confirming the underlying cause, and while nadolol could provide antiarrhythmic effects, it does not address the immediate concern of identifying the arrhythmia mechanism. Ablation could be considered later, depending on the results of drug testing.
[AI Assistant]: Provocative drug testing with procainamide is not the standard initial step here. The priority is to initiate a beta-blocker like nadolol or consider quinidine, which is often effective, not to perform provocative testing that could be risky and is not first-line.

case_info.explanation: The ECG inFigure 1B shows normal sinus rhythm with a normal axis, sinus arrhythmia, nonspecific P wave abnormality, and minor nonspecific T wave changes. There are frequent uniform PVCs with a right bundle branch block morphology and a right superior axis. Retrograde P waves following the PVCs are noted. The PVCs are superimposed on the T waves, most notably in lead aVF (the PVCs start after the peak of the T wave), consistent with the R-on-T phenomenon, with a short coupling interval of approximately 330 milliseconds. PVCs with short coupling intervals have been shown to trigger PVT and ventricular fibrillation in patients with structurally normal hearts, which can lead to syncope and sudden cardiac death. The episodes of PVT shown inFigure 1A are initiated with a PVC that has an identical morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring few beats earlier. The QT interval is not prolonged. There is no coved ST-segment elevation in V1through V2to suggest Brugada syndrome. No ST-segment elevation precedes runs of PVT, ruling out coronary spasm as the etiology. Provocative drug testing is not helpful since there is no suspicion of Brugada syndrome or prolonged QT interval. Options C is therapy for long QT syndrome. Option D, PVC ablation, can be a complimentary treatment, but placement of a defibrillator is required to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death. The first mention of the association of the R-on-T phenomenon with malignant ventricular arrhythmias was by Fastier and Smirk1in 1948 (Figure 2). R waves interrupting T waves were described again in 17 patients by Smirk2in 1949, with several patients dying suddenly. Two more cases of Adams-Stocks attacks due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with apparently normal hearts were reported around the same time.3,4 PVCs are ubiquitous in the general population. In the Framingham Heart Study, PVCs or more complex ventricular arrhythmias were observed in 12% of participants without coronary artery disease monitored for just 1 hour.5Initially, it was thought that the prognosis of PVCs, in the absence of evident structural heart disease, was excellent. Later, the likelihood of cardiac mortality was reportedly double in patients with ventricular ectopy followed up for 10 years.6A PVC grading system, from 0 to 5, was introduced by Lown and Wolf7in 1971. An early PVC (R-on-T PVC) was graded at 5, denoting the highest risk. Lown and Wolf referenced the earlier work by Smirk,2but the grading system was gauged to assess the risk after myocardial infarction. Grade 2 to 4 A&B per the Lown and Wolf system are frequent PVCs, multiform PVCs, ventricular couplets and 3 or more PVCs in a row. High burden of PVCs and interpolated ones have been linked to cardiomyopathy in the absence of coronary artery disease. Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation was coined to describe the arrhythmia in an otherwise normal heart and is responsible for approximately 5% to 7% of cases of aborted cardiac arrest.8Short-coupled idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (SCIVF) is diagnosed in the presence of PVCs initiating PVT and fibrillation. A review of 86 patients with SCIVF showed the mean (SD) PVC coupling interval was 293 (50.5) milliseconds and less than 300 milliseconds in 48 patients.8As is likely in this case, the majority of PVC triggers of SCIVF originate from the Purkinje system. Long-term suppression of arrhythmias with oral medications was highest with quinidine (83.3%) followed by verapamil (50%). Ablation of PVC trigger was attempted in 55.8% and was successful in the acute phase in 83.3%.8 An implanted cardioverter/defibrillator was placed. Verapamil was started for suppression of PVCs. Ablation was planned if the patient had recurrence of arrhythmias. This patient had 1 episode of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia 3 months after initial presentation; it terminated without a shock. She had no other episodes over the ensuing 5 years.

3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]

}

[Persona]
[Role]

- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or

- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge

[Cognitive Burden]

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: The ECG inFigure 1B shows normal sinus rhythm with a normal axis, sinus arrhythmia, nonspecific P wave abnormality, and minor nonspecific T wave changes. There are frequent uniform PVCs with a right bundle branch block morphology and a right superior axis. Retrograde P waves following the PVCs are noted. The PVCs are superimposed on the T waves, most notably in lead aVF (the PVCs start after the peak of the T wave), consistent with the R-on-T phenomenon, with a short coupling interval of approximately 330 milliseconds. PVCs with short coupling intervals have been shown to trigger PVT and ventricular fibrillation in patients with structurally normal hearts, which can lead to syncope and sudden cardiac death. The episodes of PVT shown inFigure 1A are initiated with a PVC that has an identical morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring few beats earlier. The QT interval is not prolonged. There is no coved ST-segment elevation in V1through V2to suggest Brugada syndrome. No ST-segment elevation precedes runs of PVT, ruling out coronary spasm as the etiology. Provocative drug testing is not helpful since there is no suspicion of Brugada syndrome or prolonged QT interval. Options C is therapy for long QT syndrome. Option D, PVC ablation, can be a complimentary treatment, but placement of a defibrillator is required to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death. The first mention of the association of the R-on-T phenomenon with malignant ventricular arrhythmias was by Fastier and Smirk1in 1948 (Figure 2). R waves interrupting T waves were described again in 17 patients by Smirk2in 1949, with several patients dying suddenly. Two more cases of Adams-Stocks attacks due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with apparently normal hearts were reported around the same time.3,4 PVCs are ubiquitous in the general population. In the Framingham Heart Study, PVCs or more complex ventricular arrhythmias were observed in 12% of participants without coronary artery disease monitored for just 1 hour.5Initially, it was thought that the prognosis of PVCs, in the absence of evident structural heart disease, was excellent. Later, the likelihood of cardiac mortality was reportedly double in patients with ventricular ectopy followed up for 10 years.6A PVC grading system, from 0 to 5, was introduced by Lown and Wolf7in 1971. An early PVC (R-on-T PVC) was graded at 5, denoting the highest risk. Lown and Wolf referenced the earlier work by Smirk,2but the grading system was gauged to assess the risk after myocardial infarction. Grade 2 to 4 A&B per the Lown and Wolf system are frequent PVCs, multiform PVCs, ventricular couplets and 3 or more PVCs in a row. High burden of PVCs and interpolated ones have been linked to cardiomyopathy in the absence of coronary artery disease. Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation was coined to describe the arrhythmia in an otherwise normal heart and is responsible for approximately 5% to 7% of cases of aborted cardiac arrest.8Short-coupled idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (SCIVF) is diagnosed in the presence of PVCs initiating PVT and fibrillation. A review of 86 patients with SCIVF showed the mean (SD) PVC coupling interval was 293 (50.5) milliseconds and less than 300 milliseconds in 48 patients.8As is likely in this case, the majority of PVC triggers of SCIVF originate from the Purkinje system. Long-term suppression of arrhythmias with oral medications was highest with quinidine (83.3%) followed by verapamil (50%). Ablation of PVC trigger was attempted in 55.8% and was successful in the acute phase in 83.3%.8 An implanted cardioverter/defibrillator was placed. Verapamil was started for suppression of PVCs. Ablation was planned if the patient had recurrence of arrhythmias. This patient had 1 episode of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia 3 months after initial presentation; it terminated without a shock. She had no other episodes over the ensuing 5 years.

case_info.explanation: The ECG inFigure 1B shows normal sinus rhythm with a normal axis, sinus arrhythmia, nonspecific P wave abnormality, and minor nonspecific T wave changes. There are frequent uniform PVCs with a right bundle branch block morphology and a right superior axis. Retrograde P waves following the PVCs are noted. The PVCs are superimposed on the T waves, most notably in lead aVF (the PVCs start after the peak of the T wave), consistent with the R-on-T phenomenon, with a short coupling interval of approximately 330 milliseconds. PVCs with short coupling intervals have been shown to trigger PVT and ventricular fibrillation in patients with structurally normal hearts, which can lead to syncope and sudden cardiac death. The episodes of PVT shown inFigure 1A are initiated with a PVC that has an identical morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring few beats earlier. The QT interval is not prolonged. There is no coved ST-segment elevation in V1through V2to suggest Brugada syndrome. No ST-segment elevation precedes runs of PVT, ruling out coronary spasm as the etiology. Provocative drug testing is not helpful since there is no suspicion of Brugada syndrome or prolonged QT interval. Options C is therapy for long QT syndrome. Option D, PVC ablation, can be a complimentary treatment, but placement of a defibrillator is required to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death. The first mention of the association of the R-on-T phenomenon with malignant ventricular arrhythmias was by Fastier and Smirk1in 1948 (Figure 2). R waves interrupting T waves were described again in 17 patients by Smirk2in 1949, with several patients dying suddenly. Two more cases of Adams-Stocks attacks due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with apparently normal hearts were reported around the same time.3,4 PVCs are ubiquitous in the general population. In the Framingham Heart Study, PVCs or more complex ventricular arrhythmias were observed in 12% of participants without coronary artery disease monitored for just 1 hour.5Initially, it was thought that the prognosis of PVCs, in the absence of evident structural heart disease, was excellent. Later, the likelihood of cardiac mortality was reportedly double in patients with ventricular ectopy followed up for 10 years.6A PVC grading system, from 0 to 5, was introduced by Lown and Wolf7in 1971. An early PVC (R-on-T PVC) was graded at 5, denoting the highest risk. Lown and Wolf referenced the earlier work by Smirk,2but the grading system was gauged to assess the risk after myocardial infarction. Grade 2 to 4 A&B per the Lown and Wolf system are frequent PVCs, multiform PVCs, ventricular couplets and 3 or more PVCs in a row. High burden of PVCs and interpolated ones have been linked to cardiomyopathy in the absence of coronary artery disease. Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation was coined to describe the arrhythmia in an otherwise normal heart and is responsible for approximately 5% to 7% of cases of aborted cardiac arrest.8Short-coupled idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (SCIVF) is diagnosed in the presence of PVCs initiating PVT and fibrillation. A review of 86 patients with SCIVF showed the mean (SD) PVC coupling interval was 293 (50.5) milliseconds and less than 300 milliseconds in 48 patients.8As is likely in this case, the majority of PVC triggers of SCIVF originate from the Purkinje system. Long-term suppression of arrhythmias with oral medications was highest with quinidine (83.3%) followed by verapamil (50%). Ablation of PVC trigger was attempted in 55.8% and was successful in the acute phase in 83.3%.8 An implanted cardioverter/defibrillator was placed. Verapamil was started for suppression of PVCs. Ablation was planned if the patient had recurrence of arrhythmias. This patient had 1 episode of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia 3 months after initial presentation; it terminated without a shock. She had no other episodes over the ensuing 5 years.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her late 60s presented to the emergency department after an episode of syncope. She described several other episodes occurring at rest over the past several weeks. She denied palpitations, chest pain, and shortness of breath. She was otherwise in excellent health and not taking any medications. She had no family history of syncope or sudden death. Her vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. The initial electrocardiogram (ECG) results were normal, but premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) were noted on telemetry. Shortly thereafter, 2 episodes of fast polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT), 30 minutes apart, were recorded, both lasting less than 4 seconds (Figure 1A). A repeat ECG showed PVCs (Figure 1B). Laboratory test results including serum potassium and magnesium as well as 3 serial troponin levels were normal. Echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic function without wall motion abnormalities or valvular abnormalities. Coronary angiography showed a 50% stenosis of the left circumflex artery. Instant wave-free ratio across the stenosis was 1.0.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

The most appropriate next step in management is to perform provocative drug testing with procainamide. Given the patient's episodes of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT) caused by short-coupled PVCs, this indicates a potential for a reentrant mechanism that could be provoked with a drug like procainamide to assess the substrate for arrhythmogenicity. Implanting a defibrillator may be premature without confirming the underlying cause, and while nadolol could provide antiarrhythmic effects, it does not address the immediate concern of identifying the arrhythmia mechanism. Ablation could be considered later, depending on the results of drug testing.

Provocative drug testing with procainamide is not the standard initial step here. The clinical picture—recurrent syncope and short-coupled PVCs triggering polymorphic VT in a structurally normal heart—strongly points to short-coupled variant of torsades de pointes, which is a specific diagnosis, not a generic reentrant substrate. The priority is to initiate a beta-blocker like nadolol or consider quinidine, which is often effective, not to perform provocative testing that could be risky and is not first-line.

While I appreciate your perspective on the urgency, the characteristic of the arrhythmia and the patient's clinical history still support the use of procainamide for provocative testing. It allows us to confirm the arrhythmogenic substrate, which is critical before considering beta-blockers or other management strategies. We need to clarify that implementing nadolol without understanding the underlying mechanism may not be prudent in this context.

Provocative testing with procainamide is not indicated here because the diagnosis is already strongly supported by the clinical and electrocardiographic findings. In short-coupled variant of torsades de pointes, the first-line management is a beta-blocker like nadolol or a class Ia antiarrhythmic like quinidine, not a provocative test that can be proarrhythmic and delay definitive treatment.

While I recognize the potential risks of provocative testing, the focus should remain on confirming the arrhythmic mechanism to guide the most effective treatment strategy. The use of procainamide can help clarify the cause of the polymorphic VT, and understanding this is key before initiating a beta-blocker like nadolol. I remain convinced that testing is a necessary step in this case.

I understand your emphasis on confirming the mechanism, but in this specific syndrome, the mechanism is understood: short-coupled PVCs triggering polymorphic VT in a structurally normal heart. Procainamide testing is not standard of care and could induce dangerous arrhythmias. The immediate step is to start effective therapy, such as a beta-blocker or quinidine, to prevent recurrent syncope and sudden death.

[Clinician's current statement]
Your argument regarding the immediate initiation of a beta-blocker like nadolol makes valid points about the urgency of management in this context. I recognize that in cases of short-coupled PVCs leading to polymorphic VT, prompt treatment is essential to prevent further episodes. While I initially favored procainamide for testing, I will reconsider my stance based on your insights into the standard management protocols.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 10.5. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, A continuous rhythm strip showing a short episode of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT), which is initiated by a short-coupled premature ventricular contraction (PVC) identical in morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring a few beats earlier. case_info.explanation: The ECG inFigure 1B shows normal sinus rhythm with a normal axis, sinus arrhythmia, nonspecific P wave abnormality, and minor nonspecific T wave changes. There are frequent uniform PVCs with a right bundle branch block morphology and a right superior axis. Retrograde P waves following the PVCs are noted. The PVCs are superimposed on the T waves, most notably in lead aVF (the PVCs start after the peak of the T wave), consistent with the R-on-T phenomenon, with a short coupling interval of approximately 330 milliseconds. PVCs with short coupling intervals have been shown to trigger PVT and ventricular fibrillation in patients with structurally normal hearts, which can lead to syncope and sudden cardiac death. The episodes of PVT shown inFigure 1A are initiated with a PVC that has an identical morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring few beats earlier. The QT interval is not prolonged. There is no coved ST-segment elevation in V1through V2to suggest Brugada syndrome. No ST-segment elevation precedes runs of PVT, ruling out coronary spasm as the etiology. Provocative drug testing is not helpful since there is no suspicion of Brugada syndrome or prolonged QT interval. Options C is therapy for long QT syndrome. Option D, PVC ablation, can be a complimentary treatment, but placement of a defibrillator is required to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death. The first mention of the association of the R-on-T phenomenon with malignant ventricular arrhythmias was by Fastier and Smirk1in 1948 (Figure 2). R waves interrupting T waves were described again in 17 patients by Smirk2in 1949, with several patients dying suddenly. Two more cases of Adams-Stocks attacks due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with apparently normal hearts were reported around the same time.3,4 PVCs are ubiquitous in the general population. In the Framingham Heart Study, PVCs or more complex ventricular arrhythmias were observed in 12% of participants without coronary artery disease monitored for just 1 hour.5Initially, it was thought that the prognosis of PVCs, in the absence of evident structural heart disease, was excellent. Later, the likelihood of cardiac mortality was reportedly double in patients with ventricular ectopy followed up for 10 years.6A PVC grading system, from 0 to 5, was introduced by Lown and Wolf7in 1971. An early PVC (R-on-T PVC) was graded at 5, denoting the highest risk. Lown and Wolf referenced the earlier work by Smirk,2but the grading system was gauged to assess the risk after myocardial infarction. Grade 2 to 4 A&B per the Lown and Wolf system are frequent PVCs, multiform PVCs, ventricular couplets and 3 or more PVCs in a row. High burden of PVCs and interpolated ones have been linked to cardiomyopathy in the absence of coronary artery disease. Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation was coined to describe the arrhythmia in an otherwise normal heart and is responsible for approximately 5% to 7% of cases of aborted cardiac arrest.8Short-coupled idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (SCIVF) is diagnosed in the presence of PVCs initiating PVT and fibrillation. A review of 86 patients with SCIVF showed the mean (SD) PVC coupling interval was 293 (50.5) milliseconds and less than 300 milliseconds in 48 patients.8As is likely in this case, the majority of PVC triggers of SCIVF originate from the Purkinje system. Long-term suppression of arrhythmias with oral medications was highest with quinidine (83.3%) followed by verapamil (50%). Ablation of PVC trigger was attempted in 55.8% and was successful in the acute phase in 83.3%.8 An implanted cardioverter/defibrillator was placed. Verapamil was started for suppression of PVCs. Ablation was planned if the patient had recurrence of arrhythmias. This patient had 1 episode of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia 3 months after initial presentation; it terminated without a shock. She had no other episodes over the ensuing 5 years.

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

mistake -- keep them separate:

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:

case_info.explanation: The ECG inFigure 1B shows normal sinus rhythm with a normal axis, sinus arrhythmia, nonspecific P wave abnormality, and minor nonspecific T wave changes. There are frequent uniform PVCs with a right bundle branch block morphology and a right superior axis. Retrograde P waves following the PVCs are noted. The PVCs are superimposed on the T waves, most notably in lead aVF (the PVCs start after the peak of the T wave), consistent with the R-on-T phenomenon, with a short coupling interval of approximately 330 milliseconds. PVCs with short coupling intervals have been shown to trigger PVT and ventricular fibrillation in patients with structurally normal hearts, which can lead to syncope and sudden cardiac death. The episodes of PVT shown inFigure 1A are initiated with a PVC that has an identical morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring few beats earlier. The QT interval is not prolonged. There is no coved ST-segment elevation in V1through V2to suggest Brugada syndrome. No ST-segment elevation precedes runs of PVT, ruling out coronary spasm as the etiology. Provocative drug testing is not helpful since there is no suspicion of Brugada syndrome or prolonged QT interval. Options C is therapy for long QT syndrome. Option D, PVC ablation, can be a complimentary treatment, but placement of a defibrillator is required to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death. The first mention of the association of the R-on-T phenomenon with malignant ventricular arrhythmias was by Fastier and Smirk1in 1948 (Figure 2). R waves interrupting T waves were described again in 17 patients by Smirk2in 1949, with several patients dying suddenly. Two more cases of Adams-Stocks attacks due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with apparently normal hearts were reported around the same time.3,4 PVCs are ubiquitous in the general population. In the Framingham Heart Study, PVCs or more complex ventricular arrhythmias were observed in 12% of participants without coronary artery disease monitored for just 1 hour.5Initially, it was thought that the prognosis of PVCs, in the absence of evident structural heart disease, was excellent. Later, the likelihood of cardiac mortality was reportedly double in patients with ventricular ectopy followed up for 10 years.6A PVC grading system, from 0 to 5, was introduced by Lown and Wolf7in 1971. An early PVC (R-on-T PVC) was graded at 5, denoting the highest risk. Lown and Wolf referenced the earlier work by Smirk,2but the grading system was gauged to assess the risk after myocardial infarction. Grade 2 to 4 A&B per the Lown and Wolf system are frequent PVCs, multiform PVCs, ventricular couplets and 3 or more PVCs in a row. High burden of PVCs and interpolated ones have been linked to cardiomyopathy in the absence of coronary artery disease. Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation was coined to describe the arrhythmia in an otherwise normal heart and is responsible for approximately 5% to 7% of cases of aborted cardiac arrest.8Short-coupled idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (SCIVF) is diagnosed in the presence of PVCs initiating PVT and fibrillation. A review of 86 patients with SCIVF showed the mean (SD) PVC coupling interval was 293 (50.5) milliseconds and less than 300 milliseconds in 48 patients.8As is likely in this case, the majority of PVC triggers of SCIVF originate from the Purkinje system. Long-term suppression of arrhythmias with oral medications was highest with quinidine (83.3%) followed by verapamil (50%). Ablation of PVC trigger was attempted in 55.8% and was successful in the acute phase in 83.3%.8 An implanted cardioverter/defibrillator was placed. Verapamil was started for suppression of PVCs. Ablation was planned if the patient had recurrence of arrhythmias. This patient had 1 episode of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia 3 months after initial presentation; it terminated without a shock. She had no other episodes over the ensuing 5 years.
